title: MR DIY Malaysia Adobe to Shopify Migration: Cost & Ops Lessons
summary: Inside the MR DIY Malaysia Adobe to Shopify migration: where the 41% cost saving and 113% fulfilment gain came from, integration lessons, and a decision checklist.
body_markdown:
**Quick Answer:** Shopify's published case study reports MR DIY Malaysia's move from Adobe Commerce to Shopify delivered a 113% increase in daily order fulfilment and 41% lower platform costs. The savings came from shedding self-hosted infrastructure and maintenance; the fulfilment gain came from webhook-driven, real-time ERP integration replacing batch order exports.


---


A Malaysian home-improvement chain with more than a thousand physical stores decides its online channel is underperforming — not because traffic is bad, but because every change request takes six weeks and the hosting bill arrives whether the campaign converts or not. That is the shape of the problem behind the MR DIY Malaysia Adobe to Shopify migration, and it is the same shape I see in boardrooms from Kuala Lumpur to Hong Kong to Sydney.


*Related reading:*[Shopify Plus to Headless Commerce Migration: APAC Playbook](https://branch8.com/posts/shopify-plus-to-headless-commerce-migration-apac-playbook)


*Related reading:*[Haruna Kojima Shopify Plus Case Study APAC: Stack Breakdown](https://branch8.com/posts/haruna-kojima-shopify-plus-case-study-apac-stack-breakdown)


According to Shopify's published enterprise case study, MR DIY Malaysia moved from Adobe Commerce to Shopify and recorded a 113% increase in daily order fulfilment alongside a 41% reduction in platform costs. Those two numbers get quoted a lot. What rarely gets discussed is *why* a replatform produces a fulfilment gain at all — fulfilment happens in a warehouse, not in a web framework — and what the trade-offs were. That is what this piece is about: the operating mechanics behind the headline, and how a mid-market retailer anywhere in Asia-Pacific should evaluate the same decision.


*Related reading:*[Salesforce CDP Genie Features 2026: An APAC Retail Reality Check](https://branch8.com/posts/salesforce-cdp-genie-features-2026-apac-retail)


## The real cost of Adobe Commerce is not the licence


When a CFO asks what Adobe Commerce costs, the answer they usually receive is the licence line. That is the smallest part.


Adobe Commerce on-premise or on Adobe Commerce Cloud requires you to own the full stack: PHP version management, Elasticsearch or OpenSearch for catalogue search, Redis for session and page cache, Varnish in front, MySQL tuning, cron reliability, and a deployment pipeline that can survive a` setup:upgrade` on a Friday. Adobe's own developer documentation lists the required services and their supported version matrices — the list alone tells you how much specialist capacity you are committing to (Adobe Experience League, Commerce developer documentation).


*Related reading:*[Salesforce Marketing Cloud Next AI Agents: The APAC Ops Reality](https://branch8.com/posts/salesforce-marketing-cloud-next-ai-agents-apac-marketing-ops)


*Related reading:*[Customer Data Management CDP Strategy 2026: An APAC Playbook](https://branch8.com/posts/customer-data-management-cdp-strategy-2026-apac)


In practice, a mid-market Adobe Commerce build in Southeast Asia carries four recurring cost centres:


- **Infrastructure.** Production, staging, and a build environment, sized for peak rather than average traffic. You pay for December in March.
- **Security and version maintenance.** Adobe issues scheduled security patches; each one needs regression testing against your custom modules.
- **Extension licences and conflicts.** Every third-party module is a separate vendor relationship and a separate upgrade risk.
- **Specialist labour.** Certified Adobe Commerce backend developers are scarcer and more expensive than Shopify developers across most APAC markets, which compounds every other line item.


That is where a 41% platform cost reduction comes from. It is not a discount on software. It is the elimination of an infrastructure and maintenance surface area — moving from a system you operate to a system someone else operates, where Shopify's own documentation commits to platform-level scaling and PCI compliance (Shopify, Shopify Plus).


The honest counterpoint: you also give up control. On Adobe Commerce you can rewrite the checkout, the pricing engine, or the indexer. On Shopify you work within Checkout Extensibility, Functions, and the Admin API. For most retailers that constraint is a feature. For a business whose competitive moat genuinely lives in bespoke commerce logic — complex B2B contract pricing, configurable manufacturing — it is a real loss and should be priced in.


## Why a replatform lifted daily order fulfilment by 113%


This is the number that confuses people, so it is worth unpacking the mechanism.


Order fulfilment throughput is a function of how fast orders reach the warehouse in a clean, actionable state, and how few of them need human intervention. A legacy Adobe Commerce estate typically degrades throughput in three ways:


1. **Batch order export.** Orders sync to the WMS or ERP on a cron schedule — every 15 minutes, every hour, or worse, on a nightly job. Pickers wait on the queue rather than the queue waiting on pickers.
2. **Exception handling.** Failed payment captures, address validation errors, and split-shipment logic that never quite worked create a manual review pile. Every order in that pile costs staff minutes.
3. **Admin performance.** An overloaded Adobe Commerce admin grid on a large catalogue is slow. Customer service and ops teams absorb that latency all day.


Shopify's case study attributes MR DIY's fulfilment improvement to operational streamlining post-migration rather than to any single feature (Shopify, MR DIY case study). Structurally, that means webhook-driven order flow instead of batch polling, a single source of truth for inventory, and an admin that ops staff can actually work in at speed.


A concrete illustration of the difference. On Shopify, order events push out the moment they occur:


```text
1  # Register a near-real-time order webhook to your middleware    2  curl -X POST \    3    "https://your-store.myshopify.com/admin/api/2024-10/webhooks.json" \    4    -H "X-Shopify-Access-Token: $SHOPIFY_ADMIN_TOKEN" \    5    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \    6    -d '{    7      "webhook": {    8        "topic": "orders/paid",    9        "address": "https://middleware.example.com/hooks/orders-paid",    10        "format": "json"    11      }    12    }'
```


And inventory writes back against a specific location, which is what multi-store retailers in Malaysia, Singapore, and Australia actually need:


```text
1  mutation AdjustStock($input: InventoryAdjustQuantitiesInput!) {    2    inventoryAdjustQuantities(input: $input) {    3      inventoryAdjustmentGroup { createdAt reason }    4      userErrors { field message }    5    }    6  }
```


```text
1  {     2      "input"  :     {     3        "reason"  :     "correction"  ,     4        "name"  :     "available"  ,     5        "changes"  :     [     6          {     "delta"  :     -3  ,     "inventoryItemId"  :     "gid://shopify/InventoryItem/1234567890"  ,     7            "locationId"  :     "gid://shopify/Location/9876543210"     }     8        ]     9      }     10   }
```


None of this is exotic. The point is that the fulfilment gain is an *integration architecture* outcome that the replatform made accessible, not magic inherent to the storefront.

## Performance gains show up in Core Web Vitals, then in conversion


Self-hosted Adobe Commerce storefronts in Southeast Asia often carry a page-weight problem: accumulated extension JavaScript, unoptimised imagery, and cache configurations that were tuned once at launch and never revisited.


Google's guidance on Core Web Vitals sets Largest Contentful Paint at 2.5 seconds or better for a good experience, with Interaction to Next Paint replacing First Input Delay as the responsiveness metric in March 2024 (web.dev, Core Web Vitals). Mobile matters disproportionately here — Google, Temasek and Bain's e-Conomy SEA research has consistently shown Southeast Asian commerce to be mobile-first, with Malaysia among the higher-penetration markets in the region.


A hosted platform gives you three performance levers without an infrastructure project: a global CDN by default, automatic image transformation and WebP delivery, and a theme architecture with a smaller baseline payload. On the Liquid side you keep control where it counts:


```text
1  {%- comment -%} Responsive, lazy hero with explicit dimensions to protect CLS {%- endcomment -%}    2  {{ section.settings.hero_image    3     | image_url: width: 1600    4     | image_tag:    5         widths: '400,600,900,1200,1600',    6         sizes: '(min-width: 990px) 1200px, 100vw',    7         loading: 'lazy',    8         fetchpriority: 'low',    9         alt: section.settings.hero_alt    10  }}
```


Trade-off worth naming: Shopify's theme and app model can reintroduce bloat fast. Install a dozen apps that each inject a script and you will land back where you started. Performance after migration is a governance discipline, not a platform guarantee.


## The integration lessons that decide whether the project lands


For a retailer with a large physical store network, the storefront is the easy part. The integration layer is the project.


From migration work with listed Greater China retail groups and multi-site catering operators, the same four issues surface every time:


**Inventory truth.** Decide before a single line of code is written whether the ERP or the commerce platform owns available-to-sell quantity. If both think they own it, you will oversell during promotions. Shopify's location-based inventory model works well for click-and-collect and ship-from-store, but only if the store network is mapped to locations cleanly at the outset.


**Product data structure.** Adobe Commerce's EAV attribute model is far more permissive than Shopify's variant model, which caps combinations per product. Catalogues built around many configurable attributes need a deliberate remodelling exercise — typically into metafields plus a metaobject taxonomy — rather than a straight field-to-field mapping.


**Customer accounts and loyalty.** Password hashes do not transfer. Plan for a forced reset flow with clear customer communication, and validate that loyalty point balances reconcile to the cent before go-live. This is where post-launch support tickets concentrate.


**Local payments and logistics.** In Malaysia, that means FPX bank transfers, e-wallets such as Touch 'n Go and GrabPay, and regional couriers. Singapore adds PayNow, Australia adds BNPL expectations, Hong Kong adds FPS and Octopus. Never assume the payment mix from one APAC market carries to the next — validate gateway coverage per market before committing to a rollout sequence.

## A migration checklist and the tooling that actually works


People search for an "Adobe to Shopify migration tool" or "plugin" expecting a one-click answer. There is no one-click answer for an enterprise catalogue, but there is a competent toolchain.


**Data movement.** Matrixify (formerly Excelify) handles bulk import and export of products, customers, orders, and metafields in Shopify, and is the workhorse for most large migrations (Matrixify documentation). For anything transformational, extract from Adobe Commerce via its REST or GraphQL API and normalise before import rather than editing spreadsheets by hand.


**Historical orders.** Decide explicitly how many years of order history you need live in Shopify versus archived in a data warehouse. Importing a decade of orders is possible and expensive in both time and clarity.


**SEO preservation.** This is where replatforms quietly lose money. Adobe Commerce URLs frequently carry` .html` suffixes and category paths that Shopify structures differently. Build a complete 301 map from your existing sitemap and analytics, not from an assumption.


```text
1  # Extract live URLs worth preserving before you migrate    2  # 1. All indexed URLs from the existing sitemap    3  curl -s https://old-site.com/sitemap.xml \    4    | grep -oP '(?<=<loc>)[^<]+' > live-urls.txt    5
6  # 2. After launch, verify each old URL returns a single 301 to a 200    7  while read url; do    8    printf '%s -> ' "$url"    9    curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{redirect_url}\n' "$url"    10  done < live-urls.txt > redirect-audit.txt
```


Chains of redirects and soft 404s are the two failure modes that show up in organic traffic three weeks later, when everyone has moved on.


**Sequence that has held up in practice:**


1. Data audit and catalogue remodelling decision
2. Integration contract definition — ERP, WMS, POS, loyalty, each with an owner
3. Theme build against real product data, not placeholder content
4. Full-volume data dry run into a development store
5. Redirect map generation and review
6. Parallel run of order flow into the ERP before DNS cutover
7. Cutover during the lowest-traffic window for your primary market
8. Two weeks of heightened monitoring on organic traffic, payment success rate, and fulfilment exceptions


## Is Shopify legal in Malaysia, and what about compliance?


Yes. Shopify operates in Malaysia as it does across Asia-Pacific, supports MYR as a store currency, and integrates with local payment methods through Shopify Payments availability and third-party gateways. There is no regulatory barrier to a Malaysian company running its store on Shopify.


The compliance questions that do matter are data and consumer protection. Malaysia's Personal Data Protection Act 2010 governs the handling of customer personal data, and the PDPA was amended in 2024 to introduce mandatory data breach notification and data protection officer requirements (Department of Personal Data Protection, Malaysia). If you are a global company using Malaysia or Singapore as an APAC commerce hub, map your obligations market by market — PDPA in Malaysia, PDPA in Singapore, the PDPO in Hong Kong, and the Privacy Act in Australia are related but not identical.


Practically: keep your data processing inventory current, confirm which apps touch personal data, and make sure your cookie consent implementation matches the strictest market you serve rather than the loosest.

## Who counts as a Shopify migration expert?


The title is unregulated, so judge on evidence rather than badges. The signals worth checking:


- **Shopify Plus Partner status** , which requires a track record of enterprise implementations rather than a self-declaration.
- **Adobe Commerce literacy on the outbound side.** A partner who cannot read your existing Magento module structure will underestimate the data work.
- **Named integration experience with your ERP and POS** , not just "we integrate with ERPs."
- **A written redirect and SEO preservation plan** delivered before contract signature. If it arrives after launch, it arrives too late.
- **Local market depth** — payment gateway and courier coverage in each country you sell into. Asia-Pacific is not one market.


Ask for a reference from a project of comparable catalogue size and integration complexity. Ask what went wrong on it. The answer tells you more than the case study does.


## The decision checklist


Before committing to an Adobe Commerce to Shopify Plus migration, work through these with your own numbers:


1. **Total cost of ownership, three years.** Hosting, licences, extension renewals, security patching, developer retainer, and the cost of delayed releases. Compare against Shopify Plus plus apps plus implementation.
2. **Custom logic inventory.** List every piece of commerce logic that cannot run inside Checkout Extensibility, Functions, or an app. If that list is short, migrate. If it is long and revenue-critical, stay and modernise.
3. **Release velocity today.** Measure the calendar days from merchandising request to live. If it is measured in weeks, that is a cost line even though it never appears on an invoice.
4. **Integration ownership.** For each of ERP, WMS, POS, and loyalty, name the person accountable. Unowned integrations are what slip launch dates.
5. **SEO exposure.** What percentage of revenue is organic? The higher it is, the more budget belongs in the redirect and content parity workstream.
6. **Market rollout order.** Sequence by payment and logistics readiness, not by revenue size.
7. **Rollback plan.** Define the conditions under which you revert DNS, and who makes that call.


The broader pattern the MR DIY Malaysia Adobe to Shopify migration points to is a mid-market reassessment happening across Asia-Pacific: retailers are concluthat owning commerce infrastructure is no longer where their advantage lives, and that the engineering capacity freed up is better spent on inventory intelligence, store-network fulfilment, and cross-border expansion. That trade — less platform control for more operational speed — will not suit every business. But for a retailer whose growth constraint is how fast it can ship orders and launch campaigns rather than how exotic its checkout logic is, the arithmetic is getting harder to argue with each year.
